prompt: Many companies now allow their staff to work from home for most of the week. Some people think this arrangement benefits employees, while others argue that it harms teamwork and the training of younger staff. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
The argument about home working keeps stalling because the two sides are describing different employees. Those who praise it are usually thinking of someone with fifteen years of experience and a network of colleagues already in place. Those who condemn it are thinking of someone in their first job, who has neither. Both are right about the person they have in mind.

For the experienced worker the case is close to unanswerable. A daily commute takes hours that belong to nobody, produces nothing and is paid for by the employee, and the open-plan office it leads to is an environment almost perfectly designed to interrupt sustained thought. Someone who already understands the work, and who can telephone the four people whose opinions matter, loses very little by doing it at a kitchen table. What such a person needs from an office is occasional contact, not daily attendance.

The newcomer's position is the reverse, and it is the part the enthusiasts consistently underestimate. Most of what makes an employee competent is never written down: how much certainty a claim requires before you make it, which objections a particular manager will raise, when a problem is worth escalating. This is absorbed by proximity, from half-heard conversations and from watching a senior colleague hesitate over a decision. A video call transmits the agenda and loses everything around it, and nobody schedules a meeting to pass on a hesitation.

The dispute therefore dissolves once seniority is taken into account. Judged as a single policy applied to everyone, home working is neither an improvement nor a loss but a redistribution — a transfer of time and autonomy to people who have already learned their jobs, paid for by those who have not yet learned theirs. Firms that grasp this stop debating how many days a week to require and start asking which employees the requirement is for.
title: Working from home: good for people, bad for teams?
